pos: n. (the Galician Cistercian abbey refounded in 1142, standing on the pilgrim road to Compostela)
etymology: Spanish sobrado, an upper floor or loft, from Latin superatum.
biblical_def: Sobrado dos Monxes in Galicia began as a tenth-century family monastery, lapsed, and was given to the Cistercians in 1142 at the request of Alfonso VII, settled from Clairvaux by monks sent at Bernard's direction. It stands on a branch of the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela, and its guest house has lodged walkers for eight centuries. The church was rebuilt in the seventeenth century with a Galician baroque front; the twelfth-century chapter house and the kitchen survive. The community was suppressed in 1834 and returned in 1954, and the abbey keeps a pilgrim hostel still. The dictionary records Sobrado for that hospitality, and for the correction Scripture applies to the pilgrimage it serves. Entertaining strangers is commanded with a startling reason attached, “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2). But the pilgrim standing is not earned by walking; it is the ordinary condition of every believer, “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11), and the patriarchs held it without a road to follow, “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13). What is actually being sought is not a shrine at the end of a route, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hospice would be a house of entertainment for travellers; a pilgrim as one who travels to a holy place; hospitality as the receiving of strangers; a hostel as an inn; and a wayfarer as a traveller.
webster_full: HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
HOSTEL, n. An inn; a lodging house; a place of entertainment for travelers.
WAYFARING, adj. Traveling; passing; being on a journey.
GUEST, n. A visitor; a stranger who is entertained in a house or at a table.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: Galician Cistercian abbey refounded 1142 from Clairvaux on the Compostela road, keeping a pilgrim hostel still.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lodging a stranger is commanded, whatever one makes of his reasons for walking. Sobrado has fed pilgrims for eight centuries, and the reason the epistle gives for the practice is more surprising than any route, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).

The live temptation is the pilgrimage itself, which proposes that a journey earns what Scripture gives for nothing. Peter addresses ordinary Christians by the very title the walkers are seeking, “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11); the patriarchs held the standing with no shrine to aim at, “These all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13); and the destination is explicitly not a place one can arrive at on foot, “but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

pos: n. (the Galician Cistercian abbey of 1137, called the Galician Escorial, a Trappist house today)
etymology: Spanish Oseira, from osera, a bear's den, from oso, a bear.
biblical_def: Oseira in the Galician hills was founded by hermits and made Cistercian in 1137, settled from Clairvaux, and grew into the greatest monastery of inland Galicia, called the Galician Escorial for the scale of its baroque rebuilding: three cloisters, a great staircase, and the Cloister of the Knights with its twisted palm-tree vaulting. The twelfth-century church and chapter house remain underneath the later work. It was suppressed in 1835 and reoccupied in 1929 by Trappists, who keep the strict observance there now. The dictionary records Oseira for the long devotion of a house to one place, and for the desire Scripture says such a devotion expresses. The psalmist ranks the lowest station in God's house above the best elsewhere, “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10), and gives the reason in what God is to those who walk uprightly, “the LORD will give grace and glory” (Psa 84:11). The affection is confessed rather than performed, “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house” (Psa 26:8), and the rest that is finally in view is not a cloister but a promise still open, “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a doorkeeper as one who guards an entrance; a cloister as a covered walk in a monastery; a vault as an arched roof; rest as cessation of labour; and observance as the keeping of a rule.
webster_full: DOOR-KEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a covered passage or walk round a court, usually with a colonnade.
VAULT, n. An arched roof, so constructed that the stones sustain each other; a continued arch.
REST, n. A cessation of motion or action of any kind; quiet; repose; a state of reconciliation to God.
OBSERVANCE, n. The act of observing; performance; the keeping of a rule, custom or ceremony.
scriptures: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
Psa 26:8
LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.
Heb 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
corruption_summary: Galician Cistercian abbey of 1137, the Galician Escorial, suppressed in 1835 and Trappist since 1929.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the humblest place in God's house outranks the best elsewhere, and that this is a judgment about God and not about architecture. Oseira's monks have returned to one valley twice over eight centuries, and the psalmist states the preference in the plainest terms, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10).

The live temptation is to read the preference as being about the building, which a house called the Galician Escorial makes very easy. The psalmist grounds it in what God gives, “For the LORD God is a sun and shield” (Psa 84:11); the affection is a confession rather than a discipline, “and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8); and the rest actually promised is still future and belongs to a people rather than a precinct, “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).

pos: n. (the Galician Cistercian abbey of 1154, a small house whose church survives as a parish church)
etymology: Spanish Meira, from a pre-Roman root for a boundary or a moor.
biblical_def: Meira in the Lugo highlands was settled about 1154 from Clairvaux by way of Sobrado, and it was always a small house in poor upland country, never rich, never large, never the parent of anything. Its church, built from the late twelfth century in the plain transitional manner, is the only substantial thing left of it and serves as the parish church of the village. The conventual buildings are gone. The dictionary records Meira precisely because it is small, and because Scripture takes trouble over the small. The Lord makes least things the test of great ones, “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10), and the commendation at the reckoning is pronounced over a few things and not many, “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21). The agency in anything that lasts is named so that size proves nothing, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6), and the kingdom is assigned to a condition that poverty does not disqualify, “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a priory as a convent subordinate to an abbey; upland as high land; a parish church as the church of a parish; least as smallest; and a cell in this sense as a small religious house dependent on another.
webster_full: PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey.
UPLAND, n. High land; ground elevated above the meadows and intervals which lie on the banks of rivers.
PARISH, n. The precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
LEAST, adj. Smallest; little beyond others, either in size or degree.
CELL, n. A small religious house dependent on a larger monastery; a small apartment.
scriptures: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: Small Galician Cistercian house of about 1154 whose plain transitional church is now the village parish church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture takes trouble over small things. Meira was never rich and never the mother of anything, and the Lord makes the least the assay of the greatest, “and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10).

The live temptation is the comparative one, in which a poor upland house measures itself against Poblet and finds nothing to report. The commendation in the parable is pronounced over few things, “I will make thee ruler over many things” (Mat 25:21); the agency in anything durable is stated so that scale proves nothing either way, “Not by might, nor by power” (Zec 4:6); and the kingdom is assigned where no endowment reaches, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Mat 5:3).

pos: n. (the Portuguese Cistercian abbey of 1153, the largest church in Portugal, holding the tombs of Pedro I and Ines de Castro)
etymology: Portuguese Alcobaca, from the rivers Alcoa and Baca which meet there.
biblical_def: Alcobaca in Portugal was founded in 1153 by Afonso I in fulfilment of a vow made before the taking of Santarem, and settled from Clairvaux. Its church, consecrated in 1252, is the largest in Portugal and the most austere great church in Europe: a nave over a hundred feet high with almost no ornament of any kind. The abbey kitchen had a branch of the river channelled through it. In the transept stand the tombs of Pedro I and Ines de Castro, the woman he loved and secretly married, murdered in 1355 on his father's order; when Pedro came to the throne he had her body exhumed and, by the tradition, enthroned and acknowledged as queen. The dictionary records Alcobaca for those two tombs, laid foot to foot so that the pair would rise facing one another, because that arrangement is a theology. Scripture puts the question they answer and leaves it standing in Job's mouth, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14), and fixes the sequence that no coronation of a corpse alters, “as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). The pride of such a gesture runs ahead of its fall, “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18), and the day is appointed against every exalted thing, “upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low” (Isa 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to exhume as to dig out of the earth; a transept as the cross part of a church; austere as severe, rigid; a vow as a solemn promise to God; and a bier would be a frame for carrying the dead.
webster_full: EXHUME, v.t. To dig out of the earth what has been buried; to disinter.
TRANSEPT, n. In architecture, the transverse part of a church, crossing the nave at right angles.
AUSTERE, adj. Severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to discipline and manner of life.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a solemn promise accompanied with a religious sanction.
BIER, n. A carriage or frame of wood for conveying dead human bodies to the grave.
scriptures: If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Isa 2:12
For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low:
corruption_summary: Portugal's largest church, a Cistercian foundation of 1153, holding the tombs of Pedro I and the murdered Ines de Castro.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a tomb may ask a question but cannot answer it. Pedro I laid his murdered wife's tomb foot to foot with his own so that they would rise facing one another, and the question that arrangement is reaching for is left open in Scripture by a man who knew better than to settle it himself, “all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come” (Job 14:14).

The live temptation is the royal one, which is to make a gesture do the work of a verdict. The sequence after death is fixed and no exhumation revises it, “but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27); the proverb puts the order of pride and ruin plainly, “Pride goeth before destruction” (Pro 16:18); and the day appointed falls on every exalted thing, however grieving, “For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty” (Isa 2:12).

pos: n. (the Portuguese Cistercian abbey of 1194 in the Minho, a small Romanesque house)
etymology: Portuguese Fiaes, probably from Latin filiales, dependent holdings.
biblical_def: Fiaes in the Minho in northern Portugal was a Benedictine foundation given to the Cistercians in 1194 and settled from Osera, and it remained one of the smaller Portuguese houses throughout its history, holding a modest estate on the Coura. Its church, late Romanesque with a plain west front and a single rose, survives as a parish church; the conventual buildings are mostly gone. The dictionary records Fiaes beside Alcobaca on purpose, since the two stand at the opposite ends of the same order in the same kingdom: one the largest church in Portugal with kings in the transept, the other a village church in the hills. Scripture pronounces the blessing in a way that does not favour the larger, “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3), and states the direction grace runs, “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6). The sequence that overtakes the other kind of house is stated as a rule, “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18), and the manner required of whoever has the charge of such a congregation excludes profit, “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a filial relation would be that of a dependent house; a rose-window is a circular window; modest as moderate, not excessive; a cure in this sense is the charge of souls; and a glebe as church land.
webster_full: FILIAL, adj. Pertaining to a son or daughter; becoming a child in relation to his parents.
ROSE-WINDOW, n. A circular window, with mullions radiating from the center like the petals of a rose.
MODEST, adj. Moderate; not excessive or extreme; not extravagant.
CURE, n. In church use, the charge of souls; spiritual charge; the office of a curate.
GLEBE, n. The land belonging to a parish church or ecclesiastical benefice.
scriptures: Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Jam 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Small Portuguese Cistercian house of 1194 in the Minho, its Romanesque church serving as a parish church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the blessing is not awarded by scale. Fiaes and Alcobaca belonged to one order in one kingdom and nothing could be less alike, and Christ pronounces the beatitude in terms that give the village house no disadvantage, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3).

The live temptation is the one a small house is exposed to from the other direction, a resentment that mistakes itself for humility. James fixes the direction grace actually runs, “But he giveth more grace” (Jam 4:6); the proverb states what overtakes the proud of either kind, “and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18); and the apostolic manner required of whoever has the charge excludes both coercion and gain, “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2).

pos: n. (the Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1182, named for the great waterwheel that raised the Ebro into its cloister)
etymology: Spanish rueda, a wheel, for the abbey's water-wheel on the Ebro.
biblical_def: Rueda de Ebro in Aragon was founded in 1182 by Alfonso II and settled from Escaladieu by way of Junéria, and it took its name from the engineering that made it possible: a great undershot water-wheel in the Ebro, turned by the current, which raised river water into a channel feeding the abbey's fountain, kitchen, fishpond and irrigated gardens. The wheel has been reconstructed. The abbey was suppressed in 1835 and the buildings are now a hotel and a monument. The dictionary records Rueda for the wheel, because lifting water uphill is a figure Scripture uses for the one thing men cannot do for themselves. The prophet's charge against a people is that they left a spring and dug tanks, “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns” (Jer 2:13). The river that gladdens the city is not pumped, “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psa 46:4). The tree the prophet blesses is near water rather than supplied with it, “For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters” (Jer 17:8), and the question put to all such labour concerns what it is buying, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a noria would be a water-wheel for raising water; a cistern as a receptacle for water; a conduit as a channel for conveying water; irrigation as the watering of land; and a fountain as a spring.
webster_full: WHEEL, n. A circular frame turning on an axis; a machine for raising water.
CISTERN, n. An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor.
CONDUIT, n. A canal or pipe for the conveyance of water; a duct.
IRRIGATION, n. The act of watering or moistening; the operation of causing water to flow over lands.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; the source or head of a stream.
scriptures: Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Psa 46:4
There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.
Jer 17:8

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
corruption_summary: Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1182 whose great Ebro water-wheel raised the river into its cloister.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that living water comes from a spring and not from a wheel. Rueda raised the Ebro into its own fountain by the force of the current, honest ingenuity of a kind the order excelled at, and the prophet's charge against a people is framed in exactly that contrast, “For my people have committed two evils” (Jer 2:13).

The live temptation is the cistern, which is to substitute a contrivance of one's own making for a supply one did not make. The river that gladdens the city is simply there, “the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High” (Psa 46:4); the blessed tree is near water rather than irrigated, “and that spreadeth out her roots by the river” (Jer 17:8); and the question put to the whole enterprise is about what it buys, “and your labour for that which satisfieth not?” (Isa 55:2).

pos: n. (the Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1194, set among the travertine waterfalls that give it its name)
etymology: Spanish piedra, a stone, for the travertine rock the springs deposit there.
biblical_def: The Monasterio de Piedra in Aragon was founded in 1194 by Alfonso II and settled from Poblet, in a gorge where lime-laden springs have built up terraces, grottoes and a series of waterfalls out of deposited travertine, which is the stone the place is named for. The monks dammed and channelled the water and made the first chocolate in Spain there, by tradition, from cocoa brought back from Mexico. The abbey was suppressed in 1835 and the grounds have been a park since 1840. The dictionary records Piedra for its stone, because a rock that the water itself lays down is a useful corrective to the figure. Scripture makes the rock something God puts in place and not something that accumulates, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone” (Isa 28:16). The wise builder is the one who hears and does, “which built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24). Where men fall silent the stones are said to be competent to testify, “if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40), and the water that gladdens the city of God is His own and not the monks' channel, “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psa 46:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines travertine would be a stone deposited by springs; a cascade as a small waterfall; a grotto as a natural cave; petrifaction as the conversion of substance into stone; and a spring as a fountain of water.
webster_full: CASCADE, n. A waterfall; a steep fall or flowing of water over a precipice.
GROTTO, n. A large cave or den; a natural cavern in the earth.
PETRIFACTION, n. The process of changing into stone; a substance converted into stone.
SPRING, n. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at its source.
CORNER-STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone.
scriptures: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
Psa 46:4
There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.
corruption_summary: Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1194 in a gorge of travertine waterfalls, a public park since 1840.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the rock Scripture means is laid rather than accumulated. At Piedra the stone is built up by the water itself over centuries, which is an exact inversion of the figure, and the prophet reports the foundation as God's own placing, “he that believeth shall not make haste” (Isa 28:16).

The live temptation is the slow one, in which a church supposes that what has gradually deposited around it is the same thing as a footing. Christ ties stability to hearing and doing, “Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them” (Mat 7:24); the testimony of stones is reserved for the silence of men, “I tell you that” (Luk 19:40); and the water that gladdens the city belongs to the city's God and not to the engineers, “the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High” (Psa 46:4).

pos: n. (the Swiss Cistercian abbey of 1227, keeping the most complete medieval glass cycle in Switzerland, dissolved by its canton in 1841)
etymology: German Wettingen, from an Alemannic personal name Wetto.
biblical_def: Wettingen in the Aargau was founded in 1227 by Heinrich von Rapperswil in thanksgiving for surviving a storm on the Mediterranean, and named Maris Stella. Its Gothic cloister holds the most complete cycle of medieval and Renaissance stained glass in Switzerland, some hundred and fifty panels, and its choir stalls are among the finest north of the Alps. In January 1841 the government of the canton of Aargau suppressed Wettingen and seven other monasteries by decree; the dispute over that act became one of the quarrels that led to the Swiss civil war of 1847, and the community went into exile at Mehrerau on the Bodensee, where it continues. The dictionary records Wettingen for the suppression, because a canton closing an abbey by vote raises the question of what belongs to which authority. Christ divides the two spheres and does not merge them, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21), and the civil power itself is God's ordinance and not a rival, “For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). The duty of the churchman toward the town remains, “pray unto the LORD for it” (Jer 29:7), and the fruit promised a right ordering is quiet, “the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canton as a small district; suppression as the act of putting down; a decree as an edict or law; exile as banishment; and sequestration as the seizing of property by authority.
webster_full: CANTON, n. A small portion or district of territory, constituting a distinct state or government.
SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, crushing or putting down; concealment.
DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.
SEQUESTRATION, n. The act of taking property from the owner for a time, by authority.
scriptures: They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.
corruption_summary: Swiss Cistercian abbey of 1227 with Switzerland's finest medieval glass, suppressed by the canton of Aargau in 1841.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the two authorities are distinguished and neither absorbs the other. A cantonal government closed Wettingen by decree in 1841 and the quarrel helped bring on a civil war, and the Lord's own division of the spheres is the text that was needed on both sides, “unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

The live temptation runs in both directions: a state that treats the church as its property, and a church that treats the magistrate as an enemy. Scripture grants the civil power a divine commission, “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1); it lays on the exiled churchman a duty toward the city that expelled him, “And seek the peace of the city” (Jer 29:7); and it promises a rightly ordered commonwealth quiet rather than triumph, “And the work of righteousness shall be peace” (Isa 32:17).

pos: n. (the Zurich Cistercian abbey of 1185, dissolved in 1527, and the field where Zwingli fell in 1531)
etymology: German Kappel, a chapel, from Latin capella, with am Albis for the ridge.
biblical_def: Kappel am Albis south of Zurich was founded in 1185 as a Cistercian house and dissolved in 1527 in the course of the Zurich Reformation, its revenues turned to schools and poor relief. Four years later its fields became a battlefield. On the eleventh of October 1531 the Catholic cantons surprised a small and badly assembled Zurich force beside the abbey; Zurich was routed, and Huldrych Zwingli, who had gone out with the army as chaplain, was wounded, found and killed on the field, his body afterwards quartered and burned. He was forty-seven. The dictionary honours Zwingli's recovery of preaching and his assault on the mass, and names the manner of his death as the warning it is. The church's armament is specified and the specification excludes a pike, “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God” (2Co 10:4), and the adversary named is not a Catholic canton, “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities” (Eph 6:12). Christ's word to Peter in the garden reads almost as prophecy over this field, “for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52), and Zechariah had already ruled out both of the things a general relies on, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). Luther, who had every reason to be ungenerous, said of the news only that it was a dreadful judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chaplain as a clergyman who attends an army; a cantonal league would be a confederacy; to rout as to defeat and throw into confusion; a halberd as a long-handled weapon; and a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion.
webster_full: CHAPLAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a ship of war, or to a regiment.
CONFEDERACY, n. A league or covenant; a contract between two or more persons, bodies of men or states.
ROUT, v.t. To defeat and throw into confusion; to overthrow and put to flight.
HALBERD, n. A military weapon consisting of a shaft with a head armed with a steel point.
MARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
scriptures: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Eph 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Zurich Cistercian abbey dissolved in 1527 and, four years later, the field where Zwingli was killed with the Zurich army.
corruption_paragraphs: Zwingli brought the Scriptures back into the pulpit at Zurich, preached straight through Matthew instead of the lectionary, and struck at the mass with real courage. The dictionary grants all of it, and names what he did next. He drove his city toward a confessional war, argued for a blockade of the inner cantons, and rode out with the army as its chaplain. He died on the field at Kappel. The apostolic specification of the church's weapons does not reach to a pike, “but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4).

The corruption is not Zwingli's alone and it is not finished. Wherever reform is pursued by the sword, or a modern politics treats the gospel as a programme to be enforced, the same step is being taken. The enemy Scripture names is not a neighbouring canton, “against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph 6:12). Christ's word to Peter in the garden settles the method for a disciple defending Him in person, “for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52), a sentence that reads as prophecy over this field. And the agency in any real deliverance is stated so that no army may claim it, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

pos: n. (the Lucerne Cistercian abbey of 1194, famous for its brickwork and its baroque choir stalls)
etymology: German Sankt Urban, for Pope Urban I, the abbey's patron.
biblical_def: Sankt Urban in the canton of Lucerne was founded in 1194 and settled from Lützel, and it is known for two things it made itself. The first is brick: the abbey ran its own clay pits and kilns and built in moulded brick on a scale unusual in Switzerland, with decorated tiles and traceried brick windows, a craft the house kept for centuries. The second is the choir stalls of 1711 and after, carved for the baroque church and reckoned among the best woodwork in the country. The abbey was suppressed in 1848 and the buildings have housed a psychiatric hospital since. The dictionary records Sankt Urban for its kilns, because an abbey that dug its own clay is the clearest case of the Cistercian doctrine of work, and of the motive Scripture assigns to it. The labour is directed past its customers, “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23), and the prayer that fits the finished thing asks for establishing rather than praise, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17). A trade has a purpose beyond its own continuance, “that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28), and the name given to those who build back what has fallen is honourable, “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach” (Isa 58:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a brick as a mass of clay burned; a kiln as a furnace for burning bricks; a stall in this sense is a seat in a choir; clay as an earth of a tenacious quality; and a mould as the matrix in which a thing is cast.
webster_full: BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine, then formed into a long square and baked.
KILN, n. A large stove or oven; a fabric of brick or stone which may be heated for burning bricks or lime.
STALL, n. A seat in the choir of a church, appropriated to a dignitary.
CLAY, n. In the popular sense, a soft earth which is tenacious and ductile when moist.
MOULD, n. The matrix in which any thing is cast and receives its form.
scriptures: Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Eph 4:28
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
corruption_summary: Lucerne Cistercian abbey of 1194 which dug its own clay and built in moulded brick, suppressed in 1848.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a craft kept for centuries is a form of obedience and not a sideline. Sankt Urban dug its clay, fired its own brick and carved its own stalls, and the apostolic motive directs the whole business past the people who paid for it, “as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23).

The live temptation is a workshop that becomes a treasury of merit, which is what Cistercian industry repeatedly turned into. Scripture leaves the finished work in God's hands rather than on a ledger, “yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17); it assigns a trade a purpose outside itself, “but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good” (Eph 4:28); and the honour it promises is for repair rather than accumulation, “The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12).
